blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Federated LLM unlearning addresses targeted knowledge removal when forget and retain data remain distributed across private clients and are inaccessible to the server. The resulting locally trained adapters encode conflicting objectives, making their aggregation fundamentally different from conventional federated optimization. A key failure mode is magnitude explosion, whereby unnormalized cross-client aggregation increases the merged update magnitude and degrades retained utility under stronger unlearning. We propose FIRM (Fisher-Informed Retention Merging), a single-round framework for stable and retention-aware server-side aggregation. FIRM uses client-local Fisher statistics as a unified sensitivity signal to construct a Fisher-normalized base merge and impose explicit control over retain-sensitive parameters. Its second-order retention projection admits a unique minimum-distance solution, while the corresponding dual scales with the number of retain clients rather than the model dimension. Experiments across WMDP, TOFU, and MUSE-HP using Zephyr-7B and Llama-3-8B show utility gains at comparable forgetting on WMDP and MUSE-HP, with metric-dependent trade-offs on TOFU. Controlled comparisons support benefits of the combined base merge and additional retention correction at selected operating points.

blocks.en:
The widespread deployment of large language models (LLMs) has made
selective knowledge removal practically important Maini et al. (2024) . Deployed models may encode personal, copyrighted, or hazardous information that must be removed after training Li et al. (2024) . Regulatory
frameworks such as the GDPR European Parliament and Council of the European Union (2016) and CCPA State of California (2018) further establish rights to erasure, while the cost of retraining
billion-parameter models makes targeted post-hoc removal the only
practical option in many settings. Despite this need, most LLM
unlearning methods assume centralized access to both the data to be
forgotten and representative retain data.

blocks.en:
A critical but under-studied setting is federated LLM
unlearning , where deletion-related data remain distributed across
private clients and cannot be transferred to the model provider under
localization constraints Liu et al. (2021) . Unlike centralized
unlearning, the server cannot jointly access forget and retain data to
optimize or validate the resulting model. Unlike standard federated
learning, client objectives are not uniformly aligned toward minimizing
a shared task loss. Forget clients produce updates that suppress
targeted knowledge, whereas retain clients provide
preservation-oriented updates and parameter-sensitivity information.
The server must therefore arbitrate between destructive and protective
signals without access to either underlying
dataset Romandini et al. (2025) .

blocks.en:
Recent work has addressed this problem through server-side aggregation
of locally trained adapters. FULM ( Zhong et al., 2025 ) , for example,
applies TIES-based sign resolution ( Yadav et al., 2023 ) within client
groups, followed by unnormalized summation of the resulting
domain-level centroids. Although this preserves data locality and avoids
additional server-side training, the merged adapter can grow with
heterogeneous contributions rather than remain calibrated to their
collective importance. We refer to this failure mode as magnitude explosion . As the aggregate update grows, it may
suppress general capabilities together with targeted knowledge,
causing retained-utility collapse. Moreover, sign-based aggregation
captures directional agreement but not the degree of parameter
importance to individual clients, and thus provides no explicit control
over retain-side damage.

Conventional adapter-merging methods do not directly resolve this
problem. TIES ( Yadav et al., 2023 ) and Fisher-weighted model
merging Matena and Raffel (2022) are primarily designed to combine
models optimized for compatible or cooperative objectives. Federated
unlearning instead combines updates with opposing functional roles: a
parameter may be sensitive on both forget and retain data, while
the corresponding task vectors favor opposing changes.
A suitable aggregation mechanism must therefore control both
the scale of the distributed update and its effect on
retain-sensitive parameters.

blocks.en:
Our Approach. We introduce FIRM , a Fisher-informed framework for stable and
retention-aware federated LLM unlearning. FIRM uses empirical Fisher Information Matrix (FIM) to quantify the parameter-wise importance of each client
update and employs it as a common signal throughout aggregation. This
allows the server to normalize heterogeneous unlearning contributions,
thereby preventing magnitude explosion, while simultaneously
protecting parameters that are important to retain clients. Hence, FIRM jointly controls update scale and a retain-side perturbation proxy
without requiring server-side access to either forget or retain data.

blocks.en: 2 Related Work
blocks.zh: 2 相关工作

blocks.en:
Machine Unlearning for LLMs. Early methods apply gradient ascent directly to
increase the loss on forget examples Jang et al. (2023) , but can
be unstable and degrade general utility. More robust formulations
regularize the forget objective using retain data, including gradient
difference Liu et al. (2022a) and KL-divergence penalties Maini et al. (2024) . Task Arithmetic Ilharco et al. (2023) subtracts a fine-tuned task vector from the pretrained model, whereas
RMU Li et al. (2024) redirects selected intermediate representations
toward random targets. These methods assume centralized access to
forget and retain data and therefore do not directly address
distributed deletion requests under data-locality constraints.

blocks.en:
Adapter and Model Merging. The adoption of LoRA Hu et al. (2022) has motivated methods for
combining independently trained adapters.
TIES-Merging Yadav et al. (2023) mitigates interference through
trimming, sign-conflict resolution, and selective merging, while
KnOTS Stoica et al. (2025) aligns adapters in a shared subspace
using joint singular-value decomposition.
Fisher-weighted merging Matena and Raffel (2022) estimates
parameter importance using diagonal Fisher information and
combines model parameters through importance-weighted averaging,
giving greater influence to models with higher sensitivity
at each coordinate.
UniFLoW Liang et al. (2026) addresses aggregation inconsistency
in multimodal federated LoRA fine-tuning: averaging low-rank
factors separately generally differs from averaging their
induced weight updates. It averages one factor and analytically
reconstructs the other through regularized least squares.
CrossEarth-Gate Cao et al. (2026) uses empirical
Fisher information for remote-sensing adaptation, aggregating
parameter sensitivities into module-level scores to periodically
select which modules to train.
FIRM applies Fisher sensitivities to a different objective:
combining updates with opposing forget and retain roles.
It couples coordinate-wise Fisher-normalized merging with
a retention-constrained projection that explicitly bounds a Fisher-weighted perturbation proxy.

FIRM follows a single-round protocol: the server broadcasts the
pretrained model, clients perform local adaptation and transmit one

participation. A retention-constrained projection then

blocks.en: 7 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 7 结论

blocks.en:
We introduced FIRM , a single-round framework for federated
LLM unlearning that combines local forget and retain updates without
server access to client data. FIRM couples Fisher-normalized merging
with retention control based on a diagonal-Fisher perturbation proxy.
The per-tensor projection formulation has a unique minimum-distance
optimum and an m m -variable dual. Experiments across two model families
show utility gains at comparable forgetting on WMDP and MUSE-HP,
with metric-dependent trade-offs on TOFU. Scale-tuned comparisons
support benefits of the combined Fisher-based design beyond global
rescaling, while matched-forgetting comparisons demonstrate additional
benefits from retention correction at selected operating points.
Future work will examine larger models, mixed-role clients, broader
heterogeneity, and the relationship between Fisher-proxy control and
actual retention.

blocks.en: Limitations
blocks.zh: 限制

blocks.en:
FIRM constrains a second-order empirical Fisher proxy rather than the
exact retain-loss change. Although this provides non-negative,
parameter-wise retention control, its fidelity depends on how well the
diagonal empirical Fisher represents the local retain-loss curvature.
Establishing tighter bounds between the proxy and the true loss change
remains an important theoretical direction.

在代理机和真正的损失变化之间建立更严格的界限

blocks.en:
Fisher diagonals are computed at pretrained reference weights 𝜽 F \bm{\theta}_{F} on a fresh bfloat16 model copy, avoiding 4-bit
NF4 quantisation noise. For WMDP and MUSE-HP, this is also
the client initialization 𝜽 0 \bm{\theta}_{0} . For TOFU, client training
starts from the expert-adapted model, while Fisher estimation
loads the original backbone without that expert adapter.
The Fisher batch size is one sequence, with 20 batches per client
and gradients reset before each backward pass. Each sequence uses
the causal-LM loss averaged over non-padding target tokens.
Its gradient is squared element-wise before averaging across
the 20 batches: F ^ c ​ ( j ) = 1 20 ​ ∑ b = 1 20 [ ∂ ℒ LM ​ ( x b , 𝜽 F ) / ∂ θ F , j ] 2 \widehat{F}_{c}(j)=\frac{1}{20}\sum_{b=1}^{20}[\partial\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{LM}}(x_{b};\bm{\theta}_{F})/\partial\theta_{F,j}]^{2} .
Thus, token-loss averaging precedes squaring, while cross-example
averaging follows squaring. Squared BF16 gradients are accumulated
in FP32 and the average is stored in BF16. Sequences are truncated
to 512 tokens; batches follow the supplied data order, cycling
if fewer than 20 examples are available. Only entries aligned

blocks.en:
FIRM introduces a one-time client-side Fisher estimation step after
local adapter training. With 20 Fisher batches, this is the dominant
client-side cost, but it is performed independently and can run in
parallel across clients. Server-side computation remains comparatively
light: the FIRM merge takes 217 s, compared with 547 s for FULM,
while the constrained dual projection adds only 1.2 s. Thus, FIRM’s
additional optimization cost is concentrated in local Fisher
estimation rather than the server-side projection.
